chapter_theme: The opening kaathai tells how Puhar's festival of Indra was founded at a sage's word by the hanging-fort Chola, why it must not be forgotten (the guardian spirit's anger), and gives the hereditary drummer's proclamation: the gods will come down, the city is to be adorned, every god worshipped by its own rite, the schools are to debate without enmity, and hunger, disease and enmity are to leave. The warning about a forgotten festival is the seed of Puhar's later loss to the sea.

cast.role: the great ascetic of the Malaya hill (Agastya by tradition; the kaathai does not name him) at whose word the festival was founded
a Chola of the past, the destroyer of the hanging fort, who asked Indra to dwell in Puhar for the festival
Indra, king of the gods, the thousand-eyed, whose festival Puhar holds
the eight groups of royal attendants, acting together at the festival
the drummer of the old hereditary house who beats the festival drum and proclaims the festival
the guardian spirit sent by Indra to remove the Chola king's distress

manimekalai:1:1-9.unit_note: Boundary moved from 16 to 9: line 9 (அமரர் தலைவன் ஆங்கு அது நேர்ந்தது) closes the founding story, and lines 10-18 are one sentence naming the gatherers and their verb (குழீஇ, 18), which the core cut at 16 split from its list.
manimekalai:1:1-9.reading: To raise the old city's renown, at the word of the great ascetic of the Malaya hill, the Chola of braceleted arms who destroyed the hanging fort bowed before the king of the gods and asked him to dwell in his city through the twenty-eight days of the festival the worthy desire, and the king of the gods agreed.
manimekalai:1:1-9.nuance: The festival is given a charter, not a date: a sage's counsel, a king's request and a god's consent. The founder is identified only by his feat (தூங்கு எயில் எறிந்த), the hanging fort that the Purananuru also gives to a Chola ancestor; the kaathai does not name the sage, whom tradition takes for Agastya.
manimekalai:1:1-9.event: At the Malaya sage's word the hanging-fort Chola asks Indra to dwell in his city for the twenty-eight days of the festival, and Indra agrees.

manimekalai:1:10-34.unit_note: Boundary moved from 16 to 9 at the start (see manimekalai:1:1-9); the unit now runs from the gatherers' list (10) through the assemblies' warning to the drummer's first blessing, ending at the sentence close கோலோன் ஆகுக! (34).
manimekalai:1:10-34.reading: Because the learned do not neglect what is due, the reckoners of the schools who each show truth, method, the good end and release, the reckoners of times, gods in disguise, speakers of many tongues, the five great assemblies and the eight groups gather and say that if the festival is forgotten the spirit that removed the king's distress will roar and torment the city and the spirit that beats and eats the wicked bound in its noose will be displeased, so let the festival of the thousand-eyed begin; the drum is taken from the Vajra temple onto an elephant's neck, and its hereditary drummer hails the city and wishes it three rains a year and a king whose rule does not let the planets leave their course.
manimekalai:1:10-34.nuance: The festival is kept out of fear as much as joy: the assemblies' reason is the guardian spirit's anger if it is forgotten, a threat the epic later fulfils, though by another hand (Manimekala deity's curse, kaathai 25). Line 34 can be read as a king whose sceptre keeps the planets in their places, so that rain and just rule are wished for in one breath; the reading of கோள் நிலை திரியா as qualifying the king's rod is mine. The schools' reckoners are listed among the festival's guests, the first sign of the debating hall of line 61.
manimekalai:1:10-34.event: The schools, the guests and the king's assemblies gather and call for the festival to begin; the drum is mounted on an elephant and the hereditary drummer begins the proclamation.

claims.claim: if the city forgets the festival, the guardian spirit that removed the king's distress will bring affliction on it
a spirit binds the wicked of the city with its noose, beats them and devours them

manimekalai:1:35-51.unit_note: Boundary moved from 50 to 51: line 50 (விழவு மலி மூதூர் வீதியும் மன்றமும்) is the object of மாற்றுமின் and பரப்புமின் in line 51, which closes the sentence.
manimekalai:1:35-51.reading: The drummer proclaims that on the good day of the island's rite of peace the thousand-eyed and the gods of four kinds and many classes will come to this city, leaving the golden city of heaven empty, as those who know the ancient order hold for certain, and he bids the people set up arches, golden pots, sprouts in golden trays and lamp-bearing images, plant areca, plantain, vanchi, flowering creepers and sugarcane, hang pearl strings on the gold pillars, and in the streets and squares change the old sand for new.
manimekalai:1:35-51.nuance: Lines 39 to 41 are hard: heaven, emptied by the gods' coming, becomes 'like this city on the day king Karikal Valavan left it', which seems to measure heaven's emptiness by Puhar's desolation at the loss of Karikalan, whether at his death or his going away the line does not say. The phrase தீவகச் சாந்தி returns in kaathai 24, where the day it is not performed is the day the city enters the sea.

claims.claim: on the festival day the gods leave heaven empty and come to dwell in the city

manimekalai:1:52-72.unit_note: Boundary moved from 50 to 51 at the start (see manimekalai:1:35-51); the unit now begins with the flags of line 52 and runs to the end of the kaathai.
manimekalai:1:52-72.reading: The drummer bids them raise flags and banners on the mansions and gates, have those who know the proper rites worship every god in its own way from the brow-eyed lord to the deity of the crossroads, bids those who know the good word of merit take their seats in the sand pavilions and halls and the debaters of the schools mount the debating hall, and part without hatred or quarrel even from those who do not share their view, for gods and men will roam together through the twenty-eight days; then, amid swordsmen, chariots, horses and elephants, he beats the drum, wishes that hunger, disease and enmity leave and rain and plenty overflow, and so proclaims the festival through the inner city.
manimekalai:1:52-72.nuance: The proclamation makes room for every cult, Saiva and local alike, and sets the schools' debate inside a civic festival under a rule of civility: dispute is allowed, enmity is not. The closing wish names hunger first, the ill the heroine's begging bowl will later answer. The ills of line 70 are those Kural 734 excludes from a land, but in other words, so there is no echo.
manimekalai:1:52-72.event: The drummer finishes his commands, beats the drum among the troops and proclaims the festival through the inner city.

claims.claim: each god is to be worshipped with its own distinct rites by those who know the way
debaters of rival schools should part without hatred or quarrel even from those who reject their view

links.note: The Purananuru poet names the ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort as a deed so great that killing is no longer the living Chola's own fame; Manimekalai's opening makes the hanging-fort Chola the founder of Puhar's festival of Indra.
links.teaches: Holding the two together shows the epic taking a Sangam war-memory of the Chola line and turning it into a sacred charter, so that a city's yearly rite rests on an ancestor's feat rather than on the reigning king.

gains.a: the epic's unnamed founder gains a lineage: he is the ancestor the Sangam court already cited by this one feat
gains.b: the poem's bare allusion to the fort-breaking ancestors gains a story in which that ancestor is Indra's ally and the patron of a festival

links.note: The assemblies warn that a forgotten festival will bring the guardian spirit's affliction on the city; in kaathai 25 the king, searching for his lost son, neglects the festival and Manimekala deity curses the city to the sea.
links.teaches: The opening warning is the plot's first prophecy, but its fulfilment shifts the punisher from the city's guardian spirit to Manimekala deity, so the epic keeps the civic threat while giving the punishment to its own Buddhist-protecting goddess.

links.note: Both epics place in Puhar a spirit that seizes the wicked with its noose, beats them and devours them; in the Silappathikaram it punishes named sins, in Manimekalai it is one of the powers the festival keeps appeased.
links.teaches: The same noose-bearing spirit changes office between the two epics: a moral police against hypocrites and false witnesses in the first becomes, in the second, a power whose goodwill depends on the city keeping its festival.

links.note: The Kural states that when the king bends justice the sky withholds rain; the drummer's blessing wishes three rains and an unswerving king in the same sentence, as things the festival must secure.
links.teaches: The Kural makes rain follow from the king's justice alone, while the festival treats both rain and just rule as gifts to be prayed for from the gods, so the epic's city does not leave the causal chain to the king.

gains.a: the paired wish in lines 33-34 gains its logic: the Kural explains why rain and the sceptre belong in one blessing
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a ritual setting in which a city, not trusting the king alone, asks the gods for both ends of it

links.note: The drummer proclaims the good day of the island's rite of peace (தீவகச் சாந்தி); in kaathai 24 a charana tells the king that on the day the rite is not performed his city will enter the sea, by Manimekala deity's word and Indra's curse.
links.teaches: The same rite named in the festival proclamation becomes, twenty-three kaathais later, the condition on which the city's survival hangs, so the decorations of the opening are already the terms of a covenant the city will break.

links.note: The Kural defines a land as one that goes on without crushing hunger, unceasing disease and destructive enemies; the drummer ends the proclamation by wishing that hunger, disease and enmity leave the city.
links.teaches: What the Kural states as the mark of a true land, the epic's city asks for once a year as a festival blessing, showing that the freedom from the three ills was felt as a gift to be renewed by rite, not a settled condition.

gains.a: the herald's closing wish gains a political measure: these three ills are exactly what decides whether Puhar is a land at all
gains.b: the couplet's definition gains a public voice and an occasion, a drum proclamation in which the city itself asks to meet it

links.note: The Kural advises not to do harm in hostility even when others act against you; the drummer bids the schools' debaters part without hatred or quarrel even from those who do not accept their view (பற்றாமாக்கள்).
links.teaches: The epic carries the Kural's rule of non-retaliation from private enmity into public doctrinal debate, making civility between rival schools a law of the city's festival.

gains.a: the herald's rule for debaters gains an ethical ground beyond festive peace: hostility harms the one who nurses it
gains.b: the couplet's counsel gains a concrete arena, the debating hall where disagreement is expected but enmity is forbidden

links.note: The festival bids the debaters of the schools mount Puhar's debating hall and part without quarrel; in kaathai 27, after Puhar is lost, Manimekalai goes among the schools of Vanji in disguise and hears each in turn without dispute.
links.teaches: The public hall of debate promised at the opening is never shown in Puhar; it returns only in another city as one renunciant's quiet hearing of the schools, so the epic moves doctrinal inquiry from civic festival to private search.

new_concepts.gloss: the festival; a public feast of a god or a town
new_concepts.label_source: the kaathai's own word: விழாக் கோள் (7, 20), விழா (26), விழவு மலி மூதூர் (50), அணி விழா (72)

source_issues: Lines 39-41 (மன்னன் கரிகால்வளவன் நீங்கிய நாள் இந் நகர் போல்வதோர் இயல்பினது ஆகி) are syntactically obscure: it is unclear whether Karikalan's leaving is his death or a departure, and how the comparison of heaven with the city runs.
Lines 9-10: whether அது நேர்ந்தது closes the founding story or runs on into கவராக் கேள்வியோர் கடவார் ஆகலின் is not settled by the text; the boundary at 9 is a sense break, not a full stop.
